newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Zairian peace talks expected over the weekend.
newsitem.headline: Zairian peace talks expected over the weekend.

text.p: The United Nations said on Thursday that South African leaders would aim to get warring parties in Zaire to accept the U.N.-proposed peace plan as a basis for their talks, expected over the weekend.
But U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said face-to-face talks would be difficult and so-called proximity talks -- separate conversations with each delegation by mediators -- might have to take place first.

South Africa plans to host the first talks between the Zairean government representatives and rebels, who took up arms in October, charging that the government was trying to expel ethnic Tutsis from Zaire. Zaire accuses neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of backing the rebels.
Eckhard said rebel leader Laurent Kabila was not in South Africa yet but was expected to arrive in Cape Town by this weekend.

Already in South Africa is Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba, the nephew and chief security adviser of Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, who indicated immediately his opposition to direct talks. He told Radio France Internationale from Cape Town that he did not expect to meet "any member of the rebellion."
"For us there are conditions, we want first of all the real people behind this aggression to show their goodwill and respect the decisions of the Security Council," Ngbanda said.
Eckhard said U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan had spoken to South Africa's deputy president Thabo Mbeki on Thursday.

"The efforts the South Africans are making is to eventually bring the two sides to face-to-face discussions," he said. "They might have to operate on a proximity basis at the outset and arriving at an agenda for discussions will be the first objective and probably a difficult objective."

The aim of the talks, he said, would be to get both sides to accept the five-point plan submitted by U.N. Special envoy Mohammed Sahnoun and endorsed by the U.N. Security Council as a basis for discussion.

The peace plan called for a ceasefire, the withdrawal of all foreign forces, including mercenaries, respect for the territorial integrity of Zaire and a peaceful settlement through dialogue and convening of an international conference.

In Cape Town, a spokesman for President Nelson Mandela said the peace initiative was on track but would not release any details. Also on hand was George Moose, the U.S. assistant secretary of state for African affairs, who held talks with South African officials.
Mandela revealed plans on Wednesday for a first meeting between the Zairean government and the rebels. But diplomats said Mandela had erred in going public and might have threatened the meeting.
Pretoria's director general of foreign affairs, Rusty Evans, told Reuters "There is a great reluctance on both sides to acknowledge that they are willing to negotiate."

The war in eastern Zaire is intertwined with the ethnic conflict between Hutus and Tutsis in Rwanda. Hutu hardliners massacred up to 800,000 minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994 before fleeing en masse into Zaire as a Tutsi-led government seized power in Rwanda.
